summary: This document defines a new Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Data Item for traffic classification. It identifies flows from frame or packet content, such as a destination address, and is designed to be extensible and reusable.

plainLanguage.summary: Until now the radio and the router could only tell traffic apart by its destination. This adds a way to also sort traffic by the urgency marking carried in its header.

questions: how does dlep classify flows by dscp
what is a dlep sub-data item
subtitle: A DLEP building block that lets a modem tell a router how to sort traffic into flows by DSCP or Ethernet priority.

tldr.problem: DLEP identifies traffic only by destination endpoint, so a router and modem cannot agree on finer-grained flows that should get different treatment.
tldr.mechanism: A new Traffic Classification Data Item (type 29) carries a traffic classification identifier and a list of Sub-Data Items. Two Sub-Data Items are defined, one listing Diffserv code points and one listing Ethernet VLAN and priority code points.
tldr.outcome: Other DLEP extensions, such as credit window flow control, can reuse this structure instead of defining their own flow identification. Ethernet matches win over Diffserv matches.

today: RFC 9892 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used by extensions such as RFC 9893.

sections.title: Why DLEP Needs Traffic Classification
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) is defined in RFC 8175. It exchanges link-related control information between DLEP peers, which are comprised of a modem and a router, and it defines a base set of mechanisms as well as support for possible extensions. DLEP defines Data Items, which are sets of information that can be reused in DLEP messaging. The DLEP specification does not include any flow identification beyond the DLEP endpoints, so flows are identified based on their DLEP endpoint.

This document defines DLEP Data Item formats that provide flow identification on a more granular basis. It enables a router to use traffic flow classification information provided by the modem to identify traffic flows based on a combination of information found in a data plane header. The Data Item is structured to allow the traffic classification information to be used with applications such as credit window flow control, as specified in RFC 9893, which gives an example of combining traffic classification and credit window flow control.

Traffic classification here is based on a DLEP destination and flows identified by either Differentiated Services Code Points or IEEE 802.1Q Ethernet Priority Code Points. The mechanism allows flows to be described in a flexible fashion and, when combined with applications such as credit window flow control, allows credit windows to be shared across traffic sent to multiple DLEP destinations and as part of multiple flows, or used exclusively for traffic sent to a particular destination and belonging to a particular flow. It also supports wildcard matching of any flow. The information is provided so that it can be extended to support other classification techniques, or used by extensions that are not related to credit windows, such as the extension defined in RFC 8651, or even 5-tuple IP flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Until now the radio and the router could only tell traffic apart by who it was going to. This adds a way to also sort it by how urgent it is.

sections.title: TIDs, FIDs and Flows
sections.content:
The Traffic Classification Data Item represents a list of flows that may be used at the same time to give different service classes to traffic sent from a router to a modem. The data plane information used to identify each flow is held in a separate Sub-Data Item. The Data Item and Sub-Data Item structures are intended to be independent of any specific use of the flow identification, such as flow control, and the Sub-Data Item structure is intended to allow for future classification types such as 5-tuple flows. While the structure of the Data Items is extensible, the actual flow information is expected to be used in an extension-dependent manner. When extensions supporting several Sub-Data Item types are negotiated, these types may be combined in a single Data Item.

Each list of flows is identified using a Traffic Classification Identifier, or TID, and is expected to represent a valid combination of data plane identifiers that may be used at the same time. Each flow is identified by a Flow Identifier, or FID, and each FID is defined in a Sub-Data Item that carries the data plane identifiers used to associate traffic with the flow. A DLEP destination address is also needed to complete the traffic classification information used in extensions such as flow control, and that information is expected to be provided in an extension-specific manner. For example, the address can be provided by a modem when it identifies the traffic classification set in a Destination Up Message using the Credit Window Association Data Item of RFC 9893. TID and FID values have modem-local scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Each set of classification rules gets a number, and each flow inside the set gets its own number too. Only the radio that assigned the numbers needs them to mean anything.

sections.title: The Traffic Classification Data Item
sections.content:
The Traffic Classification Data Item is used by a modem to provide a router with traffic classification information. When an extension requires the use of any Data Item, the Data Items, including this one, SHOULD be included by a modem in any Session Initialization Response Message. Updates to previously provided classifications, or new classifications, MAY be sent by a modem by including the Data Item in Session Update Messages. More than one Data Item MAY be included in a message to give information on multiple traffic classifiers.

The Data Item Type is 29 and the Length is variable. Per Section 11.3 of RFC 8175, Length is the number of octets in the Data Item, excluding the Data Item Type and Length fields. The length is limited by the packet data unit length supported: if the packet is limited to 1400 bytes, the length MUST NOT exceed that value, and if larger packets are supported, the maximum MUST be adjusted to be smaller than or equal to the maximum PDU. Multiple messages can be used if there is more data than fits in a single TLV.

The Traffic Classification Identifier is a 16-bit unsigned integer identifying a traffic classification set. There is no restriction on the values a modem uses, and no requirement for sequential or ordered values. Num SDIs is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the number of Traffic Classification Sub-Data Items included; a value of zero is allowed and indicates that no traffic should be matched against this TID. The Reserved field is currently unused, MUST be set to all zeros for this version and is currently ignored on receipt, which allows for future extensions.

A router receiving the Data Item MUST locate the traffic classification information associated with the TID in each received Data Item. If none is found, the router MUST initialize a new information set using the values in the Data Item; if some is found, the router MUST replace it. In both cases the router MUST also ensure that any data plane state associated with the TID is updated as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The radio sends the router a numbered set of classification rules. If the router already holds a set with that number, it replaces the old one with the new one.

sections.title: The Diffserv Sub-Data Item
sections.content:
The Diffserv Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item, whose Sub-Data Item Type is 1, identifies the set of DSCPs that should be treated as a single flow, so they receive the same traffic treatment. DSCPs are identified in a list of Diffserv fields. An implementation that does not support DSCPs and wants the same traffic treatment for all traffic to a destination or destinations would indicate zero DSCPs.

The Length is equal to three octets plus the value of the Num DSCPs field, so the maximum Length value is 3 + 64, or 67 octets. The definition can be split across several Sub-Data Items that are much smaller than this. The Flow Identifier is a 16-bit unsigned integer; the value 0xFFFF is reserved and MUST NOT be used. Num DSCPs is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the number of DSCPs carried. A zero indicates a wildcard match against any DSCP value that does not have an explicit match to a FID, and a typical use of that is mapping any DSCPs that are not explicitly mapped to a default queue.

Each DS Field is 8 bits long and carries the DSCP field as defined in RFC 2474, followed by two bits that must be zero. A router receiving the Sub-Data Item MUST validate the information on receipt, before using it, and a validation failure MUST be treated as an error. Once validated, the receiver MUST ensure that each DS Field value is listed only once across the whole Traffic Classification Data Item, not just within one Sub-Data Item, and a duplicate makes the Data Item an error.
sections.plainLanguage: This rule says that packets marked with certain urgency values are all treated as one flow, and a packet with an unlisted mark matches the default rule.

sections.title: The Ethernet Sub-Data Item
sections.content:
The Ethernet Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item, whose Sub-Data Item Type is 2, identifies the VLAN and the PCPs that should be treated as a single flow. Ethernet PCP support is part of the IEEE 802.1Q tag format, which includes a 3-bit PCP field and a 12-bit VLAN Identifier field. An implementation that does not support PCPs and wants the same treatment for all traffic would indicate zero PCPs, and could identify a VLAN to use per destination.

The Length is equal to four plus the number of octets needed for the Priority Fields. Because each Priority Field is 4 bits, the number of octets for the PCPs is computed by rounding NumPCPs up to the nearest even value and dividing by two, so the maximum length is 4 plus 8 divided by 2, or 8 octets. The Flow Identifier is a 16-bit unsigned integer, and 0xFFFF is reserved and MUST NOT be used. NumPCPs is a 4-bit unsigned integer giving the number of Priority Fields, where zero is a wildcard match against any PCP without an explicit match to a FID, and the maximum number of PCPs is 8.

The VLAN Identifier is a 12-bit unsigned integer field. The value 0x000 means the VID is to be ignored, and 0xFFF is reserved; any other value from 0x001 through 0xFFE can be used. Any explicitly mapped VLANs are matched first, and any VLANs without a mapping then fall to the default mapping. Each Priority Field is 4 bits long and indicates a PCP, and zero is a valid value for a PCP. A 4-bit Pad field is included when NumPCPs is odd, and it must be set to zero by the sender and ignored on receipt.

The router MUST validate the information on receipt, which can include usage-specific semantics such as those in RFC 9893, and it MUST ensure that each Priority Field value is listed only once across the whole Data Item. Where both Sub-Data Item Types are defined, matching on Ethernet information takes precedence: when a packet matches both a DSCP in a Diffserv Sub-Data Item and a VID and PCP in an Ethernet Sub-Data Item, the TID associated with the matching VLAN and PCP MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea for Ethernet: a rule matches a VLAN identifier and a priority value. When both kinds of rule match a packet, the Ethernet rule is used.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The formats defined in this document are only used when extensions require their use. The DLEP specification (RFC 8175) defines the handling of unexpected appearances of any Data Items, including those defined here.

The finer-grained flow identification mechanisms expose vulnerabilities similar to existing DLEP messages. An example of a threat to which traffic classification might be susceptible is where a malicious actor masquerading as a DLEP peer injects an alternate Traffic Classification Data Item, changing the mapping of traffic to queues, which would in turn cause delay, congestion, or loss in one or more service classes. Other possible threats are discussed in the Security Considerations section of RFC 8175 and are also applicable, though not specific, to traffic classification.

The transport-layer security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175, along with the latest versions of BCP 195, IEEE 802.1AE and IEEE 802.1X at the time of writing, can be applied to this document. The Layer 2 security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175 can also, with some updates, be applied to the mechanisms defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker posing as a DLEP peer could inject false classification rules, changing the mapping of traffic to queues and causing delay, congestion or loss. The transport security mechanisms of RFC 8175 help prevent that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned Data Item Type 29, named Traffic Classification, from the Specification Required range in the DLEP Data Item Type Values registry, and created a new registry named Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item Type Values. Types 1 to 65407 use Specification Required and 65408 to 65534 are Private Use. Initially 1 is Diffserv Traffic Classification, 2 is Ethernet Traffic Classification, 0 and 65535 are Reserved, and 3 to 65407 are unassigned.

The registry encompasses packet traffic classification, where standard packet header identifiers in packets or data frames indicate Quality of Service treatment, and it includes two specific entries for widely recognized identifiers used in IP and Ethernet networks. Reserved values are set aside for similar future identifiers, and requests for new entries are not expected to be frequent.

Allocations are subject to documentation of the intended use, approval by the designated expert appointed by the IESG, and the expert's checks that the value is clearly documented and unambiguous, that it does not conflict with existing work or ongoing efforts within the IETF, that any specification requesting a code point has been reviewed by the MANET Working Group or a successor mailing list designated by the IESG, and that external specifications requesting code points are publicly available, permanently archived and do not conflict with active or published IETF work.

The RFC also recommends that this registration guidance apply to every Specification Required registry in the DLEP Parameters group.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of rule types. Two are filled in, and a few experts decide if anyone wants to add more.

viz.caption: THE THREE IDENTIFIERS IN A CLASSIFICATION SET

items.title: TID
items.text: A 16-bit number the modem gives to one set of flows that may be used at the same time. The values are modem-local.

items.title: FID
items.text: A 16-bit number for one flow inside that set. The value 0xFFFF is reserved.

items.title: Sub-Data Item
items.text: The part that carries the data plane identifiers, such as the DSCPs or PCPs, that make up the flow.

items.title: Destination address
items.text: Also needed to complete the classification, and provided by the extension that uses it.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets in the Data Item, excluding the type and length fields.

fields.name: Num SDIs
fields.desc: Number of Sub-Data Items; zero means no traffic matches this TID.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero; ignored on receipt.

viz.caption: DIFFSERV TRAFFIC CLASSIFICATION SUB-DATA ITEM, FIXED PART (RFC 9892, SECTION 2.2)

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Three octets plus the number of DSCPs, so at most 67.

fields.name: Num DSCPs
fields.desc: Number of DSCPs; zero is a wildcard for any DSCP without an explicit match.

fields.name: DS Field
fields.desc: Carries the DSCP followed by two bits that must be zero.

viz.caption: ETHERNET TRAFFIC CLASSIFICATION SUB-DATA ITEM (RFC 9892, SECTION 2.3)

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Four plus the octets needed for the Priority Fields, so at most 8.

fields.name: NumPCPs
fields.desc: Number of Priority Fields, at most 8; zero is a wildcard.

fields.name: VLAN Identifier
fields.desc: 0x000 means ignore the VID and 0xFFF is reserved.

fields.name: Priority Fields
fields.desc: Each Priority Field is 4 bits and holds a PCP, with a 4-bit pad when the count is odd.

viz.caption: THE TWO SUB-DATA ITEMS SIDE BY SIDE (RFC 9892, SECTIONS 2.2 AND 2.3)

cells: A VLAN and a set of PCPs
Zero DSCPs matches any DSCP without an explicit FID
Zero PCPs matches any PCP without an explicit FID
64 DSCPs, so a Length of at most 67 octets
8 PCPs, so a Length of at most 8 octets
A 12-bit VLAN identifier; 0x000 means ignore it and 0xFFF is reserved

viz.caption: INITIAL SUB-DATA ITEM TYPE REGISTRY (RFC 9892, SECTION 5.2)

items.label: Diffserv Traffic Classification
items.desc: Lists DSCPs treated as one flow.

items.label: Ethernet Traffic Classification
items.desc: Lists a VLAN and PCPs treated as one flow.
